title: Make gradient descent fast by standardizing
prompt:
Fit least squares by gradient descent, the way the nightly rack-model job does, but fast.

1. `gradient_descent(grad, w0, lr, tol=1e-9, max_iter=100_000)` repeats w ← w − lr·∇f(w) until ‖∇f(w)‖ < tol. Return `(w, iterations, converged)`.
2. `fit_linear_gd(X, y)` fits y ≈ intercept + X·coef (X has one column per feature, no column of ones). Standardize each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, run your gradient descent on the loss ½‖Zβ − y‖²/n (with a column of ones in Z for the intercept) using lr = 1/L, where L is the largest eigenvalue of ZᵀZ/n, and convert the coefficients back to the original units. Return `(intercept, coef, iterations)`.

Loops over iterations are fine; avoid loops over data rows.
hints: Gradient descent's speed is set by κ = L/μ of the loss's Hessian. For least squares the Hessian is ZᵀZ/n. What does it look like when every column has mean 0 and variance 1?

After standardizing, the intercept column is orthogonal to the others and every feature has variance 1, so ZᵀZ/n is close to the identity (exactly the identity for one feature): κ near 1, and gradient descent converges in a handful of steps. Then, from y ≈ β₀ + Σ βⱼ (xⱼ − mⱼ)/sⱼ, read off coefⱼ = βⱼ/sⱼ and intercept = β₀ − Σ βⱼ mⱼ/sⱼ.

m = X.mean(axis=0); s = X.std(axis=0); Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), (X - m) / s]); H = Z.T @ Z / n; L = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).max(); beta, its, ok = gradient_descent(lambda b: H @ b - Z.T @ y / n, np.zeros(Z.shape[1]), 1 / L); coef = beta[1:] / s; intercept = beta[0] - coef @ m.

misconceptions.center-and-scale: Scaling alone isn't enough: an uncentered feature with a large mean makes its column nearly parallel to the intercept column, and κ stays huge. Center as well.
misconceptions.back-transform-intercept: Coefficients fitted on standardized features must be converted back: coefⱼ = βⱼ/sⱼ, and the intercept loses Σ βⱼ mⱼ/sⱼ.
